articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bipul Chandra Barman, a resident of ‘Hindu Prodhan Para’ in Panchagarh district of Bangladesh, came on medical visa for treatment at Siliguri
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bipul Chandra Barman, a resident of ‘Hindu Prodhan Para’ in Panchagarh district of Bangladesh, came on medical visa for treatment at Siliguri in West Bengal on March 20 last year, attended the hospital for two days, then went to Thakur Anukul Chandra Ashram at Deoghar and is untraceable since March 24 last year.For the ministry of external affairs (MEA), additional solicitor general Archana Pathak Dave informed the Supreme Court, which has in session of a habeas corpus petition by Barman’s wife in session, that the person remains untraceable and that the relatives must lodge a zero FIR relating to a missing person complaint with Jharkhand police at Deoghar.The wife, through her counsel, said on Jun 30 last year, the Bangladesh High Commission in Kolkata, acting on a request from MEA, issued a letter to the Bangladesh government seeking verification of a person detained in India and identified as Bipul Chandra Pradhan. In August last year, the Bangladesh foreign ministry sent a letter to the Indian home ministry confirming that Barman is a Bangladeshi citizen and has no criminal antecedents.In search of her husband, the wife travelled to India and gave representation for Barman’s release in June this year. Finding no response, she moved the SC.What was intriguing for the SC was the categorical denial by the MEA that Barman has neither been detained, arrested, nor deported by Indian authorities and that his status remains as a missing person. Dave also informed the court that Indian authorities have not communicated at all with the Bangladesh counterparts on Barman.Adding further complications to an already complicated case, the West Bengal government informed the court that Barman’s mobile phone number was found to be used by a person at Barh in Bihar, which is proximate to Deoghar in Jharkhand, the place he visited last before becoming untraceable. The CDR analysis showed his last known location was at a temple in Matigara, a place near Siliguri.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the ASG, who informed the Bangladesh Deputy High Commissioner about the detention of Barman and sought verification of his citizenship and antecedents. SC directed the Union government to file a detailed status report after examining all the leads given in the petition and the status report filed by the West Bengal government.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 5 spiritual teachers on why gratitude changes your life. Sadhguru, Gaur Gopal Das, Sri Sri Ravi Shankar, Dalai Lama, Thich Nhat Hanh
articles.summary: Gratitude is the feeling of appreciating the good things in your life, big or small.
articles.body: Gratitude is the feeling of appreciating the good things in your life, big or small. It might be a kind gesture from a friend, a beautiful day, or a moment when someone helped you out. When you stop to notice these things, your attention shifts away from what’s missing or stressful and toward what’s going well. It also helps your relationships, because people feel valued when you thank them. Studies link a regular gratitude habit with lower stress, better sleep and greater happiness.Spiritual traditions have taught this for centuries. In this article, we talk about five well-known teachers- Sadhguru, Gaur Gopal Das, Sri Sri Ravi Shankar, the Dalai Lama and Thich Nhat Hanh, and their about how gratitude can change the way we live.Sadhguru: Dropping the illusion of independenceGratitude isn't something you force or tick off a list. Sadhguru describes it as a state of being that reconnects you with life, and he says it shows up on its own once you stop believing you're independent. Most of us spend our days weighing what we have against what we want, and that leaves us anxious, greedy and short on contentment. Sadhguru, in his podcast, suggests stopping to notice how little of your life you produce yourself. You can't go a single moment without air, you eat food grown in soil you never tended, and you drink water that reached you through other people's hands. Once you see that, the ego begins to melt, and you go from demanding things from the world to simply receiving them. He says, take ten seconds before a meal, or a moment when you wake up, to acknowledge how lucky you are to be alive.Gaur Gopal Das: The tooth analogyGaur Gopal Das at an event talked about the tooth analogy. Your tongue keeps going to the one broken tooth and pays no attention to the other thirty-one healthy ones, and the mind does much the same, locking onto a single problem while missing everything that's going well. He says gratitude is a conscious choice to look wider. You don't have to deny your pain or pretend life is perfect, but your struggles shouldn't blot out what you have. Seeing the whole mouth instead of one tooth is the point. He also flips the usual order. Joy doesn't cause gratitude, he says; practicing gratitude is what brings happiness. Train your mind to look for the good, and over time you build a calm that outside events have a hard time shaking. Your circumstances stay the same, but how you experience them changes. Ordinary moments start to feel like blessings, and hard ones become chances to grow.Sri Sri Ravi Shankar: Gratitude turns into graceSri Sri Ravi Shankar's central idea is that gratitude opens the door to grace. He warns that dwelling on what you lack plants a "seed of insufficiency", which only grows more discontent. When you honestly acknowledge what you already have, he teaches, abundance tends to multiply. If that thankfulness settles in and stays, it becomes grace, meaning you receive something you didn't necessarily earn or qualify for. He sees it as a gift that flows freely to people who remain grateful. Gratitude also loosens the ego, which thrives on wanting more, whether that's money, recognition, or even peace. He points out that nobody can be ungrateful and at peace at the same time. To get there, he recommends Santosha, a deep contentment with whatever comes naturally. He also encourages being thankful for existence itself, including your body, your breath and your challenges. Gratitude for specific favours alone, he says, keeps it tied to the ego.The Dalai Lama: None of us is self-madeThe Dalai Lama's view comes through in The Book of Joy, built on his conversations with Archbishop Desmond Tutu. His main point is that nobody is self-made. We rely on a huge, mostly unseen network of people, from the farmers who grow our food to the workers who build our shelter. Gratitude, as the book describes it, is recognising everything that holds us in the web of life and makes this moment possible. Seeing that takes the edge off the isolated, fearful ego and leaves room for compassion toward everyone. He suggests a simple morning habit: when you wake up, appreciate that you have a precious human life.Thich Nhat Hanh: Seeing interbeingThich Nhat Hanh teaches interbeing, the idea that everything exists because of everything else. In Peace Is Every Step, he asks readers to look closely at ordinary things. A sheet of paper or a bowl of food holds the rain, the sun, the soil, and the labor of the people who made it. Once you see that, thankfulness comes easily, so gratitude starts with seeing clearly. He ties it straight to happiness. In Two Treasures, he writes, "Just by practicing gratitude, we can find happiness." A grateful person is rich in happiness, he says, while an ungrateful one can't find real peace, however much wealth or status they collect. His practice is hands-on. In The Miracle of Mindfulness, he describes breathing in and out while thanking your eyes, heart, lungs, and liver for working well right now, which makes gratitude something you feel in your body. Each of these books come at gratitude from a slightly different angle, but they point the same way.Whether it comes through noticing, giving back or seeing how connected we are, gratitude begins the moment we stop to appreciate what is already here.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Telangana physical education teacher retired in 2010 but never stopped teaching; at 74, S Sampath Kumar has written 55 books on yoga, fitness and language while offering yoga lessons free of charge
articles.summary: Retirement often marks the beginning of a slower phase of life, with people looking forward to spending more time at home and stepping away from
articles.body: Retirement often marks the beginning of a slower phase of life, with people looking forward to spending more time at home and stepping away from professional responsibilities. But for S Sampath Kumar, 74, retirement has meant something quite different. More than 16 years after hanging up his boots as a physical education teacher, the Telangana resident continues to teach, write and work towards making fitness and wellness accessible to more people.A former physical education teacher, karate instructor and yoga master from Karimnagar, Sampath retired from service in 2010. However, he never gave up teaching. Instead, he devoted more time to promoting health and wellness through free yoga classes, healing practices and books.According to a report by The New Indian Express, he has authored 55 books covering health, yoga, meditation, fitness and traditional martial arts. And he is not ready to stop writing yet. Sampath hopes to increase the number of books to 100, continuing to share the knowledge he has gathered through years of practice and teaching.His books cover a range of subjects, from yoga asanas and meditation techniques to fitness and martial arts. His interest in preserving knowledge also extends to language. He has written three research monographs documenting Telangana's dialects, recording the region's distinctive words, expressions, accents and meanings. Among his notable works are Dhyanam Lothullo, Telangana Pada Vaibhavam, Arogya Yoga, Telangana Palle Parimalam and Karate Nerchukundam.Offers free yoga coaching and helps people manage health problemsWriting is only one part of Sampath's post-retirement work. He also offers yoga coaching free of charge and guides people dealing with health concerns such as spondylitis and back pain through yoga practices and health advice.His classes go beyond physical exercises. They also emphasise teamwork, strength, discipline and the importance of maintaining both physical and mental well-being. For Sampath, the larger purpose is to help people understand the value of staying healthy rather than simply teaching them a set of exercises.He continues to explore different dimensions of yoga as well. One of the practices he teaches is Pavana Yoga, which includes floating on water as part of the practice.With knowledge of around 500 yoga asanas, Sampath is also planning to document them in another book. He hopes that putting this knowledge into writing will help preserve and share practices that people can learn and benefit from, as per the report.Wants to take yoga to IT professionalsEven after decades of teaching, Sampath continues to look for ways to reach new groups of people. One of his plans is to introduce yoga to IT professionals, whose sedentary work routines can affect their health.His efforts reflect a belief that knowledge should not remain confined to books or personal practice. Instead, it should reach people and help them make healthier choices in their everyday lives.Sampath says the purpose behind his continued efforts is to "distribute knowledge among people, help them stay healthy and ultimately build a healthy society.” He also appeals to people to support his mission.For Sampath, retirement has not meant stepping away from the profession he spent years building a life around. Whether through his books, free yoga lessons or efforts to preserve Telangana's linguistic heritage, he continues to find ways to teach. And with 45 more books as his target, he appears to have plenty of work ahead.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: Emirates Airlines loses appeal against Rs 1.88 lakh payout to Chandigarh man after Dubai floods disrupt flight to Italy; commission says passengers were not informed in time or offered alternative flights
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Chandigarh state consumer commission has upheld an order holding Emirates Airlines and travel portal Yatra Online liable after a man and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Chandigarh state consumer commission has upheld an order holding Emirates Airlines and travel portal Yatra Online liable after a man and his wife were denied boarding on a flight to Italy during floods in Dubai. The commission found that the passengers were not informed about the disruption in advance or offered alternative arrangements. It upheld directions to the companies to pay Rs 1.88 lakh and Rs 10,000 towards compensation and litigation costs.In its order dated October 28, 2026, the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Chandigarh, dismissed Emirates Airlines' appeal against the district commission's order dated May 4, 2026, holding both companies jointly and severally liable.Why were passengers denied boarding?According to the commission order, Raghav Jain, a Chandigarh resident, booked tickets for himself and his wife through Yatra Online for travel from New Delhi to Milan via Dubai on April 19, 2024. Their return journey was scheduled from Thira, Greece, to New Delhi via Dubai on May 10. He paid Rs 1,45,384.99 for the booking.Jain alleged that when they reached Delhi airport on April 19, they were denied boarding because of flight disruptions caused by floods and adverse weather conditions in Dubai. He said neither company had informed them sufficiently in advance or arranged an alternative flight.He claimed that he was forced to buy last-minute tickets on Saudia Airlines for Rs 2,13,103.87. He also alleged that he lost a day's business opportunities and Rs 23,600 paid towards prepaid accommodation.The complainant further alleged that Yatra failed to reissue their return tickets despite repeated follow-ups. He said the companies initially indicated that Rs 54,938.50 would be refunded but later reduced the amount to Rs 24,582. He approached the consumer commission alleging deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.What did Emirates sayThe Emirates attributed the disruption to unprecedented floods and storms in Dubai between April 14 and 19, 2024, which had left thousands of passengers stranded at the airport.It argued that public notices about restrictions on transit passengers had been issued through social media, its website and other online platforms, given the circumstances, individually informing every affected passenger was not feasible.The airline maintained that the restrictions were imposed for passenger safety and convenience and sought dismissal of the complaint.Yatra's defence was struck off by the district commission on November 12, 2024, for failing to file its written version within the prescribed period.Commission's findingThe bench of president Justice Raj Shekhar Attri and member Preetinder Singh said adverse weather conditions could explain flight disruptions but did not absolve the airline of its responsibility to inform passengers and arrange suitable alternatives.It noted that Jain and his wife were informed about the disruption on April 19, the day of travel, when they had already reached Delhi airport. Emirates failed to establish that they were informed earlier or offered an alternative flight.“The issuance of general public notices, without evidence of effective communication concerning the complainant’s booking, does not displace these findings,” the commission observed.It also noted that the airline itself had stated that floods and storms had affected Dubai from April 14. However, the embassy advisory relied upon by Emirates was issued only on April 19.The bench said that had the couple been informed on April 14 or 15, they could have made alternative arrangements and avoided the last-minute inconvenience and additional expenditure.“The failure to establish timely intimation, despite the commencement of the adverse weather conditions several days before the scheduled journey, consequently resulted in avoidable mental agony and harassment to the complainant and his wife,” it said.The commission found that the district commission had correctly calculated the additional expenditure at Rs 1,88,521.87 after deducting the Rs 24,582 refund from the cost of alternative tickets. It found no legal infirmity warranting interference.Final orderThe state commission dismissed Emirates' appeal and upheld the directions requiring both companies, jointly and severally, to pay:Rs 1,88,521.87 towards additional expenditure on alternative tickets, with 9 percent annual interest from the date of filing the complaint until payment.Rs 10,000 towards mental agony, harassment and litigation costs.The district commission had stipulated that failure to comply within 45 days of receiving its certified copy would attract 12 percent annual penal interest on the principal amounts from the expiry of the deadline until payment. The state commission dismissed the appeal without imposing additional costs.

articles.title: $12 billion battle for US Congress: Musk, Soros and other billionaires pour in cash
articles.summary: The 2026 US midterm election campaign is expected to become the most expensive in the country's history, with total spending projected to reach nearly $12
articles.body: The 2026 US midterm election campaign is expected to become the most expensive in the country's history, with total spending projected to reach nearly $12 billion, according to Opensecrets, an independent organisation that monitors campaign finances.A significant share of the expenditure is being driven by outside political groups, particularly super political action committees (Super PACs), which are investing heavily in key electoral contests ahead of the November 3 election.Billionaire businessman Elon Musk has emerged as the biggest individual donor, contributing nearly half a billion dollars to support republican candidates. Much of his spending has focused on Texas, where several of his companies are headquartered.BBC Verify has examined the campaign finance figures to assess how much has been spent, who is funding the candidates and where the money is going.The president says he has held 31 rallies over 27 days, along with many tele-rallies, a term that's been used recently in US media to describe when a politician phones into a rally.How much money has been spent?US campaign finance regulations place limits on the amount individuals, political parties and traditional political action committees (PACs) can contribute directly to candidates.However, Super PACs can accept unlimited donations from individuals, corporations, labour unions and other political committees. Although they cannot donate directly to candidates, they can independently spend money to support or oppose them.The latest filings with the federal election commission (FEC), covering spending up to mid-October, show that more than $9.5 billion had already been spent during the current election cycle.PACs and Super PACs accounted for more than half of the expenditure, contributing approximately $5.5 billion. Their spending almost doubled over the preceding couple of months.Candidates, political parties and outside organisations are required to report their expenditure to the FEC. However, the complete figures will only become available after the elections.Based on spending patterns from previous election cycles, Opensecrets estimates that the final amount could reach $11.9 billion. This would represent an increase of around 30% compared with the 2022 midterm elections.Who are the biggest political donors?According to the liberal-leaning Brennan Center for Justice, the 40 largest donors had contributed a combined $2.4 billion by October 14, marking a record amount for this stage of a midterm election cycle.Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert, said the 2026 elections had broken spending records, with an increasing proportion of the money coming from wealthy individuals and organisations.Apart from individual contributions, organisations also provide substantial funding to PACs. Geosor Corp and the Fund for Policy Reform, both established by billionaire financier George Soros, have together donated $102 million to liberal groups.Former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been another major democratic donor, contributing more than $60 million.On the Republican side, several wealthy contributors have made large donations. These include Jeff Yass, head of a major trading firm, and business supply company owners Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, who have collectively contributed more than $100 million to Republican causes during the campaign, according to FEC records.Musk, however, remains the biggest individual contributor, having donated nearly $500 million as of October.A large portion of his contributions has gone to America PAC, a Super PAC he established in 2024, as well as the republican-aligned senate leadership fund.Much of the funding has been directed towards the Texas Senate contest, where republican candidate Ken Paxton is facing democrat James Talarico.America PAC has invested more than $45 million in the Texas race. It has also allocated approximately $10 million each to senate contests in Michigan and Ohio.The cryptocurrency industry has also emerged as a significant contributor this election cycle. Brendan J Glavin of Opensecrets said ripple and coinbase had together donated $63 million to Super PACs seeking to advance the interests of the crypto sector.Where is the campaign money being spent?Political campaigns and outside groups use their funds for a range of activities, including recruiting workers for grassroots voter outreach, organising rallies and other campaign events, and conducting internal opinion polls.However, advertising accounts for the largest share of campaign expenditure, particularly television commercials.According to advertising tracking firm AdImpact, $11.15 billion had been spent on political advertising by the end of October.Beckel said traditional broadcast television continued to receive the largest share of advertising expenditure, although spending on digital platforms was also increasing.AdImpact's tracking showed that the biggest advertising investments were concentrated in Senate contests in Michigan, Texas and Ohio, followed by Iowa and Maine.You use AI every day. articles.body: MEERUT: A 30-year-old man died during treatment on Sunday night after allegedly consuming a poisonous substance following a dispute with his wife and in-laws. An eight-minute video recorded by him before his death has also surfaced, in which he named his wife and several members of her family, holding them responsible for his condition.The deceased, Prabal Kumar Gupta, was a resident of Patelpuri in the Kankerkhera police station area. His father, Rajiv Gupta, a BJP functionary and resident of the same locality, suffered a heart attack after learning about his son's death. He was rushed to a private hospital, where he is undergoing treatment.Circle officer Daurala Shiv Thakur said, "The man died by suicide following a dispute with his wife and in-laws. The matter was already under mediation through the police, and counselling had been conducted to resolve the differences between the couple."Prabal married Sneha Gupta, a resident of Rishinagar on Rohta Road in the TPNagar police station area, on November 2, 2025. According to family members, differences had developed between the couple soon after their marriage. The two also attended a counselling session at the women's police station on Saturday in an attempt to resolve their marital dispute.According to his family, Prabal left home on his scooter around 11am on Sunday. He allegedly consumed a poisonous substance during the day and recorded a video before being found unconscious in the Sadar police station area. Local residents rushed him to Kailashi Hospital in Kankerkhera. After providing initial treatment, doctors referred him to Subharti Hospital due to his critical condition. He died during treatment there on Sunday night.In the video that surfaced after his death, Prabal spoke about the circumstances leading to his decision and named his wife, Sneha Gupta, her father, brother, aunt and other relatives, holding them responsible for his condition. He also referred to the counselling session held at the women's police station.Shiv Thakur said, "No formal complaint has been received in the matter so far. We are awaiting the postmortem report, while the allegations levelled against police personnel in the video are also being verified. articles.title: Thief enters locked First AC coupe, steals Rs 8 lakh jewellery; couple claims no police response despite 3 alarm chain pulls at Lucknow station
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: A couple travelling with their one-year-old child in a First AC coach of a train alleged that gold jewellery worth Rs 7-8 lakh and around Rs
articles.body: LUCKNOW: A couple travelling with their one-year-old child in a First AC coach of a train alleged that gold jewellery worth Rs 7-8 lakh and around Rs 35,000 in cash were stolen from their locked coupe at Lucknow's Charbagh railway station in the early hours of November 2.Despite repeated calls to the railway helpline and pulling the alarm chain three times, no GRP or RPF personnel turned up to assist them at the station, the couple claimed.The incident occurred around 1.20am aboard train number 15726, when Umesh Kumar, 31, his wife Sunita Kumari, 30, and their child were travelling from Anand Vihar to Deoria on berths E13 and E14 of H1 coach.Umesh, who works with a private firm in Delhi, married Sunita in 2023. The family, originally from Bhore in Bihar's Gopalganj district, was heading home to celebrate Diwali and Chhath.Speaking to TOI, Umesh said he had fallen asleep on the upper berth while his wife and child were sleeping below. The coupe was locked from inside."My wife suddenly woke up and saw a tall, heavily built man dressed in black standing inside the coupe. He appeared to be putting something into his pocket. When she noticed him, he apologised, claiming he had mistakenly entered the wrong cabin, and walked away," Umesh said.Within a minute, Sunita discovered that her purse had been ransacked and the jewellery and cash were missing."The jewellery was purchased during our wedding. Its present value would be Rs 7-8 lakh. Around Rs 30,000-35,000 in cash was also stolen," Sunita told TOI.Umesh claimed that the intruder had managed to open the coupe door from outside despite its being locked internally.He said police personnel who subsequently met them at Gonda station demonstrated how the door could be opened from outside even when locked from within.Following the theft, Sunita alerted the onboard travelling ticket examiner (TTE), while the couple pulled the alarm chain repeatedly to stop the train from leaving Lucknow."Despite pulling the chain three times and making several calls, no policeman came to help us at Charbagh. We first encountered police personnel at Gonda after contacting emergency helpline 112," Umesh alleged.According to the National Train Enquiry System (NTES), the train, running one hour and 40 minutes late, arrived at platform number two of Charbagh station at 1.15 am and departed for Gonda at 1.35am. The GRP and RPF police stations are located on platform number one.Trains ordinarily have RPF or GRP personnel deployed for security duties. However, it could not immediately be ascertained whether a security squad was present aboard this particular train.Umesh claimed he contacted railway helpline 139 around three times, but the operators only registered his complaint and provided a reference number. No immediate assistance followed, he alleged."By the time they forwarded the complaint, the train would have left the station. I kept asking them how that would help us," he said.The couple subsequently lodged a Zero FIR with GRP Deoria around 9am on November 2.GRP Charbagh SHO Dharamveer Singh told TOI, "We have reached out to the victim to ascertain the sequence of events. The probe is on. The Zero FIR copy is yet to be received from GRP Deoria."TOI also attempted to contact the onboard TTE, from whom the couple had sought assistance, but his phone was switched off.Umesh further claimed that he had noticed frequent movement through the connecting doorway between the First AC coach, the 19th coach from the locomotive, and an adjoining general coach during the journey. He said the doorway was repeatedly opened and closed.Meanwhile, a video of Sunita narrating the incident has surfaced on social media. In the video, she expressed anguish over the lack of police assistance despite repeated calls and alarm chain pulling."This is Yogi's govt, yet there has been no response. Tell me, what am I supposed to do? Nobody is coming to help us. If we are not safe even inside a locked cabin, where will we be safe? Fortunately, my child was not abducted. What would I have done if someone had taken my child?" Sunita said in the video.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: A Wisconsin father gave his son a stake in the family car dealership, but a feud over ownership and company money lasted more than a decade; an appeals court upheld $321,330 in civil-theft damages against the son
articles.summary: A family business can become the centre of a bitter dispute when questions over ownership, financial decisions and control begin to divide relatives.
articles.body: A family business can become the centre of a bitter dispute when questions over ownership, financial decisions and control begin to divide relatives. In Wisconsin, a disagreement between a father and son over a family-owned car dealership continued for more than a decade, eventually leading to multiple lawsuits, allegations of misuse of company funds and a court-ordered dissolution of the business. What began as a family ownership arrangement ultimately resulted in the son being held personally liable for civil theft.In its October 30, 2026, decision in Carl Schneider v. Chris Schneider, available on Justia, the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit upheld a judgment against Chris Schneider, rejecting his challenge to $321,330 in exemplary damages awarded for three instances of civil theft. The appeals court found no clear error in the lower court's conclusion that he had knowingly used company money for purposes he was not authorised to pursue. The ruling also addressed his argument that an earlier lawsuit prevented the trust from seeking certain damages again.How a family dealership became the subject of an ownership disputeThe dispute centred on Hybrid Car Store Inc., a car dealership in La Crosse, Wisconsin, founded by Carl Schneider in 1976. His son, Chris, became the company's general manager about a decade later. Carl initially gave Chris a 25% ownership stake, while Carl and his wife, Narcelle, each retained 37.5%. The family later established the Carl and Narcelle Schneider Trust as part of their estate planning, transferring their respective ownership interests into it. This gave the trust a 75% stake in the company.The situation changed in 2008 when Narcelle transferred her 37.5% interest from the trust to Chris, making him the majority shareholder with 62.5% ownership. Carl challenged the transfer in state court in 2014, arguing that it violated the estate arrangements and that Chris had breached his fiduciary duties. The state court ruled that the transfer violated certain agreements and ordered Chris to pay $562,500 for the ownership interest he had improperly received. It also directed him to pay the trust $56,250 in withheld dividends, along with interest.Company money used to settle personal obligationsAccording to the Seventh Circuit's account of the case, Chris subsequently arranged for the company to provide him with a loan of $281,196.61 and a dividend payment of $281,303.39 to help satisfy the state-court judgment. He then used company-issued payments to pay the amounts owed to the trust. The dispute continued when the company later indemnified Chris for $395,574.81 in legal expenses from the earlier state-court proceedings. He used the money to repay the company loan and took the remaining amount in cash. However, Chris did not repay the company the $56,250 drawn from its account.Another disagreement arose over the dealership's property expenses. The company had repaved its parking lot and replaced its roof in 2012. Carl alleged that Chris improperly attributed those expenses to him personally rather than to the company. In 2018, Chris negotiated the sale of the dealership to Dahl Automotive. During the negotiations, he arranged a monthly rent subsidy of $15,000 for Dahl without informing the trust. After the dealership was sold in March 2019, the company was made to pay these subsidies. The trust also alleged that Chris failed to distribute the dealership sale proceeds to the shareholders.Court finds three instances of civil theftCarl and his daughter, Mary Schneider, acting as trustees, filed the federal lawsuit in December 2019. They accused Chris of improperly obtaining company loans, breaching his fiduciary duties and committing civil theft. After reviewing the evidence and conducting a bench trial, the US District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin found Chris liable for several financial irregularities.The court identified three instances of civil theft: using $56,250 in company funds to satisfy his personal state-court judgment, directing the company to pay $191,500 in rent subsidies promised to Dahl Automotive, and using a dividend intended for the trust to cover a disputed promissory note created in 2021. The court found that Chris had arranged for a promissory note to be created in Carl's name for the earlier roof and parking lot expenses, despite Carl having no knowledge of it. The arrangement allowed Chris to use the trust's share of a company dividend to cover the disputed promissory note, while receiving a corresponding dividend himself.Under Wisconsin law, civil theft can result in exemplary damages when the required elements of theft are established. The district court awarded the trust $321,330 in exemplary damages for the three incidents. It also ordered the company to pay the trust $553,905.49, directed the company's dissolution and appointed a receiver to oversee its affairs.Seventh Circuit rejects son's argumentsChris challenged the findings, arguing that he believed he had authority to make the payments and had attempted to repay the money. He also maintained that an earlier federal lawsuit involving the dealership's roof and parking lot expenses prevented the trust from pursuing related damages again. The Seventh Circuit rejected both arguments. The appeals court explained that the 2021 promissory note and the subsequent dividend arrangement involved new actions that occurred years after the earlier litigation. Therefore, the previous case did not prevent the trust from pursuing claims arising from those later events.On the civil-theft findings, the court agreed that Chris knew the company was not responsible for his personal judgment or the rent subsidies he had promised Dahl. It also found sufficient evidence that he knew he lacked authority to use company funds through the disputed promissory note arrangement. The court further clarified that an intention to repay money later does not provide a defence to theft under the relevant Wisconsin statute.The appeals court declined to review the separate damages judgment against the company because Chris lacked standing to challenge it. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the amended judgment against Chris Schneider and remanded the case for the limited purpose of determining the trust's attorney fees and costs incurred during the appeal. The ruling was issued as a nonprecedential disposition, meaning it is not binding precedent in other cases.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Australian company ordered to pay $191,859 after hackers used a supplier’s compromised email account to redirect invoice payments to a fake bank account
articles.summary: An Australian company has been ordered to pay a supplier more than $190,000 after hackers changed the bank details on an invoice and redirected the
articles.body: An Australian company has been ordered to pay a supplier more than $190,000 after hackers changed the bank details on an invoice and redirected the payment. Inoteq Pty Ltd had hired electrical contractor Mobius Group to carry out work on a Rio Tinto project. In 2022, when Inoteq prepared to pay the invoices, it received emails from Mobius’s hacked systems containing new bank account details. The company transferred the money to the new account, not realising that the details had been changed by hackers.Inoteq later argued that it should not be held responsible for the lost money. According to ABC News, the District Court of Western Australia rejected its argument, finding that the company had failed to take enough steps to confirm the new bank details.Hackers sent fake bank details from Mobius’s compromised email systemMobius Group, an electrical contractor, had agreed to carry out work for Inoteq Pty Ltd on a Rio Tinto project. In March and April 2022, Mobius sent Inoteq invoices totalling $235,400. However, on the day Inoteq was preparing to make the payments, a hacker sent emails from Mobius’s compromised systems.The first email appeared to come from Mobius’s director and provided new bank details, asking Inoteq to update its records. The change raised concerns at Inoteq, so a staff member called Mobius to verify the details. However, the poor phone connection prevented them from confirming the change. Inoteq then emailed Mobius asking for proof of the new account details. The hacker replied to that email without either company realising that the response was fraudulent.Supplier discovered the fraud after contacting Inoteq about unpaid invoicesThe fraud was discovered about a week and a half later, when Mobius contacted Inoteq about the unpaid invoices. Police were called after the companies realised what had happened. By that stage, some of the transferred money had been sent overseas. However, $43,541 was recovered. A cybersecurity expert who gave evidence in the case said the scammer had accessed the email account of Mobius’s director. This meant Inoteq could not have identified the messages as fraudulent from the email address alone. The expert said a phone call was needed to verify the changed bank details. Mobius later began legal action to recover the remaining $191,859 from Inoteq.The court ordered Inoteq to pay the remaining $191,859 with interestInoteq argued that it should not be held responsible for the loss. It pointed to an indemnity clause in its contract and claimed that Mobius had failed in its duty of care by not adequately protecting its email accounts. However, Judge Gary Massey rejected both arguments.The judge acknowledged that Inoteq had taken a sensible step by calling Mobius to verify the new bank details. However, the call did not confirm the change because of the poor phone connection. He said Inoteq should have made another call instead of relying on the email response. Since it failed to do so and transferred the money to the fraudulent account, the court ordered Inoteq to pay the outstanding $191,859, along with 6% annual interest.False billing scams a growing concern for Australian businessesThe case has drawn attention because false billing scams are common and the decision may influence similar disputes across Australia. Australian Competition and Consumer Commission data cited in the report recorded 13,120 reports of false billing scams in 2020. That figure rose to 39,587 in 2023. Lawyer Andrew Bower said the case was, to his knowledge, the first reported decision involving fraudulent updated bank details sent solely from a legitimate email address that had been compromised.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information, including the report published by ABC News and details of the court proceedings. The Times of India has not independently verified the claims, financial transactions, or other details mentioned. The information is based on the reported findings and the court's decision in the case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A £100 Japanese chest became a London engineer’s TV stand for 16 years; linked to Cardinal Mazarin, it resurfaced and sold for €7.31 million
articles.summary: A 17th-century Japanese lacquer chest, once a humble TV stand in London, has been rediscovered and sold for €7.31 million, linked to Cardinal Mazarin. Learn about its fascinating history and remarkable auction story.
articles.body: Few pieces of furniture have carried as much hidden history as the black-lacquered, gold-decorated chest that sat under a television in a South Kensington flat from 1970 until 1986, according to The History Blog. Its owner first used it as a stand for his television and later turned it into a bar for keeping drinks. No one in the room knew that the very same chest had once travelled from Japan to Europe and ended up in the collection of a French cardinal. That changed in 2013, when a French auctioneer entered a house in the Loire Valley and recognised the piece standing in the corner of a room. It was sold at auction that year for €7.31 million.A £100 purchase in South KensingtonA 17th-century Japanese lacquer chest, once owned by Cardinal Mazarin, was used as a television stand in a London home for 16 years before being discovered. It sold at auction in France in 2013 for €7.31 and went to Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum. According to The History Blog, the flat’s landlord was Zaniewski, a Polish doctor and the tenant was an engineer who worked for Shell Petroleum. The Engineer kept the chest as a stand for his television for 16 years, from 1970 until he retired to the Loire Valley in 1986, where he turned it into a bar.From a Kyoto workshop to Cardinal Mazarin The chest dates back to 1640 and was manufactured in Kyoto, most likely in the workshop of Kōami Nagashige, who was the official lacquerer to the Tokugawa rulers, according to the Rijksmuseum. The History Blog says that these lacquer chests were ordered by François Caron, head of the Dutch East India Company’s office in Japan. The Daily Mail said the chest is about 4 feet 8 inches wide and that only about ten remain. Victoria and Albert Museum notes that the chest depicted scenes from the Tale of Genji and the Tale of the Soga Brothers.A ban on exporting such lacquered chests came into effect in 1641, but because Caron was grandfathered in, the items were exported in 1643. In the company’s records for that year, four extra-large lacquer chests are mentioned. The chest belonged to Cardinal Jules Mazarin, chief minister of France from 1642 to 1661 and an important art collector. He acquired the two largest chests in Amsterdam and shipped them to France aboard a warship. Mazarin’s family kept the chests until the French Revolution, when a haberdasher brought this one to a sale and passed the chest to the English collector, William Beckford.Seventy years out of sightThe trail went cold in 1941. In 1941, during the Second World War, an auction at Llantarnam Abbey listed it simply as a large Chinese chest and its link to Cardinal Mazarin and its Japanese origin was forgotten. From then onwards, the largest of the cardinal’s gold chests was deemed lost. The Victoria and Albert Museum, which owns another of these chests, kept searching and, in the end, another just turned up at the State Historical Museum in Moscow. As the Daily Mail pointed out wryly, the missing chest was actually under a TV, a few hundred yards away from the museum.The appraisal in Touraine In the wake of the engineer's death, his family approached the Rouillac auction house to value his Touraine property. Philippe Rouillac, the auctioneer, discovered that the bar was a 17th-century chest from Japan made of gold, silver, copper and mother-of-pearl. A late 19th-century photograph he compared it to helped confirm that it was one of the four chests purchased by Mazarin. The initial estimate with bidding set to open at €200,000.A winning bid and a Dutch homeThe sale took place at Cheverny on 9 June 2013 and the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam won it. The Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties recorded the winning bid of €7.3 million for a chest found in a private house in France. The chest achieved a hammer price of €5.9 million, making it the highest auction sale in France that year. Additional buyer fees of approximately €1.4 million brought the final price to €7.31 million, the Antique Trade Gazette reported. It was purchased by the museum with the help of the Jaffé-Pierson Foundation, the BankGiro Lottery and Vereniging Rembrandt. The curator of the Rijksmuseum, Menno Fitski, referred to it as “the best of the best,” ArtFix Daily reported. The chest, which first reached Europe through Amsterdam, was back in Dutch public possession.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1983, Cadbury buried 12 clue boxes for its Creme Egg hunt; one finder’s 22-carat egg later rose from £6,500 to £123,500 at auction
articles.summary: Discover the incredible story of Cadbury's 1983 Creme Egg treasure hunt, where a buried 22-carat gold egg sold for £123,500 at auction, transforming from a £6,500 find into a remarkable investment. This article explores the Conundrum concept, the historic treasure hunt, and the egg's unique features.
articles.body: Long before treasure hunts moved onto smartphones, Britain had one that came wrapped in chocolate advertising. In the early 1980s, people armed with spades and a book of riddles were poking around historic sites and private land, hoping to dig up a gold egg. More than four decades later, one of those eggs is back in the headlines. A Dorset man dug it up and it sold at auction in 2018 for a hammer price of £6,500; in August 2026, it sold again for a hammer price of £123,500, Lincs Online reported.A book of riddles and twelve buried eggsTo promote its Creme Eggs, Cadbury came up with a treasure-hunt concept that saw Garrard & Co, crown jewellers to the British royal family for more than 160 years, craft 12 individual golden eggs, National Jeweler and JCK reported. The 12 perspex cases containing wooden boxes and letters were hidden at various undisclosed locations across the country. The treasure hunters had to solve the puzzles and conundrums found in the book titled Conundrum: The Cadbury’s Creme Egg Mystery, which was authored by Don Shaw and illustrated by Nick Price.The egg Clive Pinder dug up in Somerset As reported by the BBC, Clive Pinder, from Dorset, cracked the clues that led to Cricket St Thomas, Somerset, in 1983 and recovered the casket containing the egg known as Cuckoo Cuckoo. The egg is made of 22-carat gold with green and blue enamel. It depicts a cuckoo sitting in a tree, surrounded by seven human figures. Seven wheat sheaves are also embossed on its back, along with Garrard & Co.'s maker's mark and a London hallmark for 1983. Lincs Online said Cuckoo Cuckoo weighs about 253 g and stands 8 cm high. The treasure hunt became so disruptive that the Weekly Dispatch cancelled it after six weeks, following reports of roads being dug up, trees damaged and public spaces vandalised.How £6,500 became £123,500Pinder sold the egg at auction in 2018 for a hammer price of £6,500. Its buyer later put it up for sale again. On 1 August 2026, Batemans of Stamford, Lincolnshire, sold the egg for a hammer price of £123,500. Lincs Online reported that the egg had been estimated at £15,000 to £20,000, so the hammer price was more than six times the top estimate. It was nearly 19 times the hammer price of 2018, but one should note that hammer price and premium-inclusive totals are not equivalent figures.Greg Bateman, managing director of the auction house, told Lincs Online that the sale was absolutely incredible and that the conundrum eggs were a fascinating piece of British cultural history. The provenance of the item was a factor here as well because the lot had everything it needed: the green leather presentation box, the original perspex box which had been buried, the wooden conundrum casket, the original handwritten parchment letter and the 1983 version of the book.A market that keeps climbingCuckoo Cuckoo is not the first time a conundrum egg has shocked the market. A bigger thirteenth egg, given to a Cadbury retailer through a contest, instead of being discovered by the public in an egg hunt, was sold for £37,200 with buyer's premium in 2021, according to the Guernsey Press, compared to the £20,000 from the 2017 sale. Cadbury Creme Eggs are still sold each Easter, while the gold egg outlived the hunt in which it was hidden.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2006, Volvo buried a pirate-themed XC90 in the Bahamas; 52,000 Americans joined the hunt and all 7 finalists received new cars
articles.summary: In 2006, Volvo buried a pirate-themed XC90 V8 in the Bahamas, inviting 52,000 Americans to participate in a thrilling treasure hunt. The challenge drew massive interest and concluded with all finalists winning new cars, marking a unique promotional collaboration with Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean.
articles.body: Most people who buy a car worry about where to park it. In 2006, Volvo took the opposite approach and buried one, then dared the public to find it using online clues. The vehicle was a one-of-a-kind, pirate-themed XC90 V8 hidden somewhere in the world and the only way to claim it was to dig it up. Volvo’s July 26, 2006 press release said more than 52,000 people in the United States took part in the hunt. David Hutz of Virginia eventually located the buried SUV, but Volvo surprised all seven finalists by awarding each of them a new vehicle.Why did Volvo bury an SUV?It was Volvo’s official campaign for the release of Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man’s Chest. The buried XC90 V8 SE Lux would have cost £46,325 in Britain, Fleet News reported. Volvo billed the hunt as the first search for a buried car. The participants could take a free map from one Volvo dealer and sign up online. The hunt started on June 12, 2006 and ran for four weeks. The participants had to solve some online clues and puzzles and Fleet News claimed that puzzles were sent to registered players via email and became more difficult as time passed during the competition. Almost 30,000 people had entered within the first two weeks, Volvo said, and more than 52,000 Americans took part in the end. Maps and registration stayed open until July 11 and a final clue on July 12 closed the online stage.Seven finalists and a secret island These people were the first contestants from their respective countries to solve the final riddle. There were three from America, including Jenny Buckalew from Newman, Georgia; David Hutz from Herndon, Virginia and James Hutz from Carefree, Arizona. Others included Karl Lloyd from England, Susanne Kalintsch from Austria, Akihiro Horibe from Japan and Jose Luis Dominguez Monge from Spain.Volvo arranged flights for all seven finalists to an undisclosed location on August 6, 2006. The company also provided travel and accommodation for one guest accompanying each finalist, according to a contemporary report by The Auto Channel. According to Volvo’s press release, the finalists did not learn where the final stage would take place until their plane landed in the Bahamas. They had to solve both physical and mental tasks in order to be eliminated or come closer to the car, according to the chief marketer.The dig, the keys and the twistDavid Hutz, a 30-year-old computer programmer, figured out the final destination. His team found the SUV on Abaco Island, Bahamas, on August 9 and handed him the keys. He immediately handed the vehicle to his wife, Sheila, who had travelled with him, Volvo said in a photo caption. Hutz said he had stayed up all night working out the riddles. The surprise didn’t end there. Volvo made it a point not to reveal that all the finalists would receive a prize. Each finalist was stunned by receiving a chest of gold containing keys to a brand-new Volvo, as reported by the VolvoXC site.What the stunt achievedThis was followed up by Volvo with webisodes, telling the tale of the final hunt on 24th August. To build interest in the contest, Volvo Cars of North America published an article on June 28 about the greatest treasure hunters of all time. According to the Volvo UK press release reproduced by Automotoportal, there were more than 1 million hits on its website. It also included statements by Hugh Reid, the UK managing director of Volvo, who called it one of the most unique and successful movie tie-in promotions ever done by a car manufacturer.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2006, Judge Judy Sheindlin and her daughter started a mentoring programme with just eight or nine girls; 20 years later, it has involved around 1,500 young women and more than 1,000 volunteer mentors
articles.summary: When Judge Judy Sheindlin and her daughter Nicole Sheindlin launched Her Honor Mentoring in 2006, it began with a modest group of eight or nine
articles.body: When Judge Judy Sheindlin and her daughter Nicole Sheindlin launched Her Honor Mentoring in 2006, it began with a modest group of eight or nine high-school girls and a simple belief: a trusted professional woman could help a young person see a wider future for herself. Twenty years later, the programme has grown into a regional mentoring network involving approximately 1,500 mentees and more than 1,000 volunteer mentors, according to Fox News and Her Honor Mentoring.The programme’s growth is impressive, but its purpose has remained remarkably consistent. Her Honor connects motivated high-school senior girls, many of whom are first-generation college-bound students from families with limited financial resources, with mentors who can offer practical guidance on education, careers, confidence and money. What began as a small experiment has become a structured nine-month experience designed to open doors that might otherwise remain closed.How the programme beganNicole Sheindlin has described the programme as a reflection of her own relationship with Judge Judy. After attending the same law school as her stepmother, she later sat beside her in family court, where she saw the influence a strong professional woman could have on a young person’s outlook and opportunities. That experience became the model for Her Honor.The idea was not simply to give girls advice. It was to create sustained relationships between young women and mentors from different professional worlds, allowing mentees to ask questions, test ambitions and learn how to navigate education and work. Judge Judy and Nicole concluded that they could help young women gain extra skills and expand their professional networks by building a programme around that kind of connection.The first class was tiny. Judge Judy recalled that it included only eight or nine participants, while the most recent class in September had more than 100. That growth did not happen overnight, but it shows how a small, well-designed programme can scale when schools, businesses and volunteers see its value.Who Her Honor servesHer Honor works with high-school senior girls nominated by their schools. The organisation says its mentees are first-generation, college-bound students from families with limited financial resources, a focus that places the programme where mentorship and professional networks can make the greatest difference.Participants are not left to work things out alone. Her Honor pairs mentors and mentees carefully, taking into account interests and life experiences in order to build relationships based on trust and relevance. The programme’s stated aim is to create a productive and inspiring mentoring relationship rather than a one-off meeting or a generic career talk.The programme now operates across the Bronx, Westchester and Rockland counties in New York, with a pilot initiative in Burlington, New Jersey. Its growth from eight students at one high school to more than 100 students across multiple schools reflects both rising demand and the involvement of local schools, businesses and community organisations.What mentors actually doThe core of Her Honor is a nine-month hybrid mentoring experience focused on college and career readiness. Mentoring teams meet weekly throughout the academic year, guided by the Her Honor curriculum and arranged at times and places that fit busy schedules.The curriculum goes beyond academic achievement. Mentees work on communication, problem-solving, time management and accountability, while also receiving support around college applications, career exploration and professional presentation. In practice, that can mean learning how to write an email, prepare for an interview, manage deadlines or think seriously about life after high school.Financial literacy is another central part of the experience. Judge Judy told Fox News that participants are paid for working and learn how to dress for success, make first impressions, manage money and become financially prepared for adulthood. The combination of practical work, mentoring and financial education is intended to give young women tools they can use long after the programme ends.Why the model worksMentorship often succeeds because it gives young people access to knowledge that is not always available at home or school. A mentor can explain how a workplace operates, what college life is really like, how to handle setbacks or how to ask for help without feeling embarrassed. Those conversations can change how a student imagines her own future.Her Honor also recognises that confidence is practical, not abstract. Former mentee Keiry Alvarez said the programme helped her overcome timidity, while her mentor Lilliana Mendoza said Her Honor helped her gain people skills, find her voice and receive guidance that influenced her career as a police officer. These personal accounts show how the programme’s structure translates into everyday confidence.The programme’s impact extends to mentors as well. Nicole Sheindlin said mentors have discovered that giving back supports their own wellbeing, while Judge Judy noted that several former mentees have returned as mentors after beginning their careers. That cycle turns a mentoring programme into a community habit, where each generation helps prepare the next.A network, not just a programmeOne of Her Honor’s strengths is the breadth of its volunteer base. Fox News reported that more than 1,000 mentors have taken part from 400 organisations and businesses over the programme’s 20-year history. That range exposes mentees to careers and professional environments they may not otherwise encounter.The organisation describes mentoring as a way to bridge education gaps with local business resources. Its philosophy is that investing in young people is essential to building healthy, equitable and resilient communities, and the involvement of companies and professionals gives that philosophy practical form.The current 2026 to 2027 class includes 108 mentees and 123 mentors across 14 schools in the Bronx, Rockland and Westchester counties. The fact that mentors slightly outnumber mentees reflects the programme’s team-based approach, in which guidance is shared rather than delivered by a single adult.Twenty years of second chancesJudge Judy has spent much of her public life dealing with conflict, dysfunction and difficult decisions. Her Honor offers a different kind of legacy, one built on prevention, encouragement and practical opportunity. She told Fox News that seeing young women still hoping, dreaming and working hard renews her faith in people.The programme’s numbers tell one part of the story: 1,500 mentees, more than 1,000 mentors and 31 high schools involved over two decades. But its deeper achievement may be quieter. It has helped young women develop the confidence, skills and relationships needed to pursue education and work with greater purpose.Her Honor began with a handful of girls and a mother-daughter partnership. Two decades later, it has become proof that mentorship, when done consistently and thoughtfully, can create a cycle of opportunity that reaches far beyond its first classroom.You use AI every day. articles.title: The 'villa scam': Rajasthan govt issues show-cause notices to IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal, IPS wife Prashakha Mathur over resort bought below market rate
articles.summary: JAIPUR: Rajasthan govt has issued show-cause notices to senior IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal and his IPS officer wife, ADG Prashakha Mathur, regarding
articles.body: JAIPUR: Rajasthan govt has issued show-cause notices to senior IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal and his IPS officer wife, ADG Prashakha Mathur, regarding alleged discrepancies in their immovable property declarations.The notices, which require responses within seven days, are based on charges that the couple and their close family members purchased 40 resort villas from a single company at allegedly below-market rates. The notices were issued by the department of personnel (DoP) on Oct 30, seeking clarification on why properties acquired post-2021 were omitted from the immovable property declarations submitted by the officers.According to the DoP notice, the Agrawals had failed to declare any new immovable properties in their online statements since 2021, even though they submitted communications to the state govt under the All-India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1986, regarding property transactions completed after that date.In a related development, the commissionerate of industries and commerce Monday suspended incentives previously approved for Goyal Fashions Pvt Ltd, the company at the heart of the investigation.The suspension, ordered following intervention from chief minister Bhajan Lal Sharma, will prevent the company from receiving any investment incentives or concessions until ACB concludes its inquiry into the matter. It has ramped up its preliminary investigation into the alleged irregularities involving Agrawal and Mathur, issuing notices to various govt departments, district administrations, banks and private entities to obtain records related to the couple. This includes a notice served on Sanjay Goyal, managing director of Goyal Fashions Pvt Ltd, which operates the Ananta chain of hotels and resorts.Sources in ACB suggested that the bureau is examining property registration records and other documents concerning the luxury villas acquired by the Agrawals at Ananta resorts. “Various other transactions at the company’s Bujhda resort in Udaipur and Ajabgarh resort in Alwar, including purchases allegedly made at prices substantially below market rates, are being examined,” an ACB source said.The bureau has also reached out to the industries department, requesting minutes from meetings held during Agrawal’s tenure as its additional chief secretary, as well as reports on departmental decisions to ascertain whether any official actions had unduly benefitted Goyal Fashions.Previously, the bureau also sought information from the public works department regarding the construction of villas and cottages at the company’s sites in Udaipur and Alwar, and investigated allegations of relaxed construction conditions and approvals granted to the company without due verification of necessary certificates.ACB initiated its preliminary inquiry against Agrawal on Oct 30 after securing necessary approvals from the state govt under Section 17-A of the Prevention of Corruption Act. articles.title: In Oklahoma, discarded dumpsters have been transformed into Hazmatt, a 20-foot-tall reclining robot holding a wildflower; the city spent just over $14,000 on the public artwork unveiled in January 2026
articles.summary: What happens when discarded dumpsters are given a second life?
articles.body: What happens when discarded dumpsters are given a second life? In Norman, Oklahoma, they have been turned into a 20-foot-tall robot that reclines on a hillside, holding a wildflower in one hand. Called Hazmatt, the unusual public sculpture transforms retired waste containers and reclaimed materials into an artwork designed to encourage people to rethink their relationship with rubbish and the environment. The City of Norman funded the multi-year project with just over $14,000 from leftover construction funds, and the sculpture was officially unveiled in January 2026.According to an announcement by the City of Norman dated December 12, 2025, Hazmatt was created by Kenneth Eugene Hall Jr., a Norman-based artist and founding member of Crucible Art Foundry and Gallery. The sculpture stands at the city's Household Hazardous Waste Facility, where it serves as a reminder that materials often treated as waste can still have a purpose.A giant robot built from discarded wasteUnlike conventional public sculptures made from bronze, stone or steel, Hazmatt was constructed almost entirely from retired dumpsters and reclaimed waste materials. The project brought together the idea of recycling with an imaginative design, turning objects associated with rubbish collection into a giant figure with a distinctly relaxed appearance. Hazmatt's reclining posture is central to its message. Rather than depicting a robot in an aggressive stance or dramatic action pose, the sculpture appears to be resting on the hillside, holding a wildflower. The contrast between the imposing size of the figure and the delicate flower gives the installation a gentler character.The city describes Hazmatt as a “gentle giant”, with its relaxed and contemplative posture intended to encourage residents to consider their connection with the environment. Its construction also demonstrates how discarded materials can be repurposed rather than sent directly for disposal. Roadside America, which documented the installation following its unveiling, identifies local artists Ken Hall Jr. and Derek Vosten in connection with the sculpture. The travel website describes Hazmatt as being assembled from dozens of old dumpsters. The city's original announcement, however, names Hall Jr. as the sculpture's creator.How much did the city spend on Hazmatt?The sculpture's reported cost is another notable aspect of the project. The City of Norman said the multi-year undertaking was funded at just over $14,000, using leftover construction funds from its Household Hazardous Waste Facility Capital Project. The city used money remaining from the facility's construction project to support an installation that also reflects the site's environmental purpose. The city said all fabrication and assembly took place either at the facility itself or at the city's Container Maintenance Facility. This connected the sculpture's creation to the municipal operations that handle waste and maintain city equipment.Hazmatt was officially dedicated during a ribbon-cutting ceremony on January 13, 2026, at 3803 Chautauqua Avenue. A subsequent report by Hoodline said the event included remarks from Mayor Stephen Tyler Holman, City Manager Darrel Pyle, artist Ken Hall Jr. and Derek Vosten, among others. The city's council meeting records also refer to the ribbon-cutting and describe the sculpture as a creative, cost-effective alternative to disposing of decommissioned dumpsters.Why the robot stands at a hazardous waste facilityThe sculpture stands at Norman's Household Hazardous Waste Facility, which began operating in 2022 and provides residents with a place to dispose of or recycle materials that require special handling. According to the city, the facility accepts items including pesticides, kerosene and paint removers. Such products cannot always be treated like ordinary household rubbish, making appropriate collection and disposal important for environmental protection.By placing the sculpture at the facility, the city has connected a public artwork with a practical waste-management service. Visitors arriving to dispose of household hazardous materials encounter a giant figure built from discarded objects, reinforcing the idea that responsible waste handling begins with considering what happens to unwanted materials.Michele Loudenback, manager of the city's Division of Environmental Resilience and Sustainability, said Hazmatt would act as a friendly ambassador for visitors to the facility. In the city's announcement, she described the installation as an example of waste reduction and resourcefulness. The sculpture's message is therefore not limited to recycling alone. Its design encourages people to think about how everyday decisions, including the disposal of potentially harmful products, affect the environment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Diwali cleaning tips: How to remove dust, stains and odours from mattresses, pillows and cushions at home
articles.summary: With Diwali on November 8, the annual clean-up is in full swing, and guests will soon be sitting on your sofa cushions and sleeping on your beds.
articles.body: With Diwali on November 8, the annual clean-up is in full swing, and guests will soon be sitting on your sofa cushions and sleeping on your beds. Mattresses, pillows and cushions are easy to forget, yet they collect dust, sweat, oil, spills and odours all year round. The good news is that you do not need special equipment or harsh chemicals. A vacuum cleaner, baking soda, mild detergent and a sunny afternoon can bring them back to life. Here is a simple five-step guide to cleaning them at home before the festival.Start with the care labels and a good airingBefore you clean anything, check the care label. Mattresses, memory foam, feather pillows and decorative cushions with embroidery or beads all need different care. Take off covers, sheets and pillowcases, and wash them in hot or warm water if the label allows. Then carry the mattress, pillows and cushions to a sunny, airy spot, or prop them up near an open window. Sunlight and fresh air help freshen fabrics and reduce damp smells. Two to three hours in the sun is usually enough.Vacuum away dust and mitesDust and dead skin settle deep in the fabric, which is why a simple vacuum makes such a difference. Use the upholstery attachment and go over the whole mattress, including the seams, edges and underside, then the pillows and cushions. Move slowly and press lightly so the suction can reach into the folds. Do the same for the sofa seams and the spaces behind the cushions. Regular vacuuming every month or two keeps dust build-up low and helps people with dust allergies.Lift stains gentlyTreat stains early, and always blot rather than rub, since rubbing pushes the stain deeper. For fresh liquid spills, press a clean, dry cloth on the spot to soak up the moisture. For sweat, oil or food marks, mix a little mild detergent with water, dab it on with a cloth and blot with a clean damp cloth. A paste of baking soda and a few drops of water also helps lift marks on mattresses and cushions, left on for 15 to 20 minutes before vacuuming off. Avoid soaking the mattress or foam, since trapped moisture can lead to mould.Freshen with baking sodaBaking soda absorbs odours, which makes it ideal for mattresses, pillows and cushions that smell stale. Sprinkle a thin, even layer over the surface and leave it for at least an hour, or a few hours if the smell is strong. Then vacuum it up thoroughly. For a fresher scent, you can add a few drops of an essential oil to the baking soda before sprinkling, but test a small hidden spot first, and keep it away from children and pets. Do not use vinegar and bleach together, and avoid strong chemicals on mattresses.Dry fully and protect for the futureEverything must be completely dry before it goes back on the bed or sofa. Damp fabric attracts mould and smells, so give each item enough time in the sun or a well-ventilated room, and turn it over halfway. Once dry, put on fresh covers, and consider a washable mattress protector and pillow protectors for future protection. Wash pillowcases and bedsheets weekly, air your mattress every few months, and turn or rotate it if the manufacturer recommends it. A little regular care means less effort before the next Diwali.Disclaimer:This article is intended for general informational and household purposes only. Results vary with the type of fabric, filling and stain, and individual technique. Always follow the manufacturer’s care instructions, and test any cleaning product on a small, hidden area first. Avoid soaking mattresses, memory foam and delicate fabrics, never mix cleaning products, and keep them away from children and pets. People with allergies or asthma should take care when handling dust. For severe stains, mould or pest problems, consult a professional cleaner.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 4-time Rampur MLA, ex-SPG commando Nand Lal dies at 72 in Shimla
articles.summary: SHIMLA: Former Congress MLA from Rampur Bushahr and Chairman of the Seventh Himachal Pradesh State Finance Commission Nand Lal died at Chamiyana Hospital
articles.body: SHIMLA: Former Congress MLA from Rampur Bushahr and Chairman of the Seventh Himachal Pradesh State Finance Commission Nand Lal died at Chamiyana Hospital in Shimla early Tuesday following a prolonged illness. He was 72.Nand Lal, who represented the Rampur Assembly constituency for four consecutive terms between 2007 and 2022, breathed his last around 5 am. His death has triggered an outpouring of grief among political leaders and residents of the region.Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu expressed grief over the veteran leader's demise and conveyed his condolences to the bereaved family.In a condolence message, the chief minister prayed for eternal peace for the departed soul and strength for the family to cope with the loss.The message, shared through a tribute poster, read: "May God grant the departed soul a place at His feet and provide the family with the strength to bear this immense sorrow."Born on April 16, 1954, in Devthi village of Rampur Bushahr in Shimla district, Nand Lal had a career spanning security services and electoral politics. He was the son of Pyare Lal and held a postgraduate degree in Political Science from Himachal Pradesh University, Shimla.He began his professional career after receiving training with the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), where he served as a commando. In 1985, he joined the Special Protection Group (SPG), the elite security organisation tasked with protecting the Prime Minister and other designated protectees.Nand Lal served with the SPG until 1997 and was assigned several important security responsibilities, including being part of the security detail of Congress leader Sonia Gandhi. His association with the Gandhi family earned him the description of "Sonia's sentinel" in media reports.He was also involved in security arrangements for several major national and international events, including the 1982 Asian Games, the 1983 Non-Aligned Movement meeting and the 1984 Commonwealth conference.During his service, he also commanded ITBP battalions twice in terrorism-affected areas of Jammu and Kashmir, working in challenging operational conditions.After several years in the security services, Nand Lal took voluntary retirement in 2007 and entered electoral politics. He contested his first Assembly election from Rampur Bushahr on a Congress ticket and won.He went on to represent the constituency in four consecutive Assembly elections in 2007, 2012, 2017 and 2022. In the 2022 elections, he defeated BJP candidate Kaul Singh Negi to secure his fourth consecutive victory.His political career remained closely linked to the Congress organisation in Himachal Pradesh and development issues concerning Rampur Bushahr and neighbouring areas.Nand Lal served as Chief Parliamentary Secretary (CPS) in the state government from 2013 to 2017. Between 2018 and 2022, he was associated with the Assembly's Welfare and Rural Planning committees. He also served on various legislative committees, including as chairman of the Privileges Committee.In March 2024, the Governor appointed him chairman of the Seventh Himachal Pradesh State Finance Commission.The commission was tasked with examining the financial position of Panchayati Raj institutions and urban local bodies and making recommendations on the distribution of financial resources and strengthening local governance.As chairman, Nand Lal was associated with reviewing the financial requirements of local bodies and their capacity to provide development and civic services.He was married to Satya Devi and is survived by his son.Nand Lal represented Rampur Bushahr in the Himachal Pradesh Assembly for 15 years. His journey from the security services to electoral politics saw him take on responsibilities in national security, legislative affairs and local governance.His four consecutive Assembly victories, tenure as Chief Parliamentary Secretary and appointment as chairman of the State Finance Commission marked significant milestones in his public career.His demise has left a void in the political landscape of Rampur Bushahr, with Congress leaders, political representatives and residents mourning the loss of a veteran leader who remained closely associated with the region throughout his political career.(With Agency Inputs)Stay updated with the latest Shimla news.
